# Slides That Carry a Decision {#sec-slides}

```{python}
#| label: slides-setup
# The evaluation's results (scripts/evaluation.py), and the deck and theme as this chapter
# leaves them (checkpoint 16; later chapters move the colours into a brand file), with the
# theme's contrast computed by the formula of its own test.
import json
import re
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path

from scripts import evaluation as ev
from scripts.prose import alt_text_holds, number_words, text_holds
from scripts.wcag import contrast, scss_variables

S = ev.summary()
best = S["best_version"]
WORD = number_words()
recall = ev.value(best, "recall_top10")["value"]
share = Fraction(S["top_share"]).limit_denominator(100)
text_holds(share == Fraction(1, 10), "\"a tenth of the list\" in the headline title")
headline = f"{best} reaches {ev.percent(recall)} of subscribers by calling a tenth of the list"

CHECKPOINT = ev.PROJECT.parents[1] / "checkpoints" / "16-eval-slides"
scss = (CHECKPOINT / "acme.scss").read_text()
# The colours the theme gives each role, resolved as tests/test_deck_contrast.py resolves them.
theme = scss_variables(scss)
ROLES = {"body": "$body-color", "headings": "$presentation-heading-color",
         "links": "$link-color", "captions, footer": "$text-muted"}
colour = {role: theme[var] for role, var in ROLES.items()}
paper = theme["$body-bg"]
ratios = {role: contrast(c, paper) for role, c in colour.items()}
text_holds(min(ratios.values()) >= 4.5, "every text colour the test checks passes 4.5:1")
deck = (CHECKPOINT / "slides.qmd").read_text()
n_slides = 1 + len(re.findall(r"^## ", deck, re.M))
text_holds(n_slides == 8, "the deck's eight slides")

# The titles as rendered, by media/capture/eval_outputs.py (step deck): if stale, rerun it.
captured = json.loads((Path(ev.__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "media" / "figures"
                       / "eval-deck-titles.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
TITLES = captured["titles"]
text_holds(len(TITLES) == n_slides and TITLES[1] == headline, "the captured titles")
# Every number the captured titles print, rebuilt from outputs/ as the deck builds it, so a
# capture older than the results stops the render (rerun eval_outputs.py, step deck).
releases = [r["version"] for r in S["releases"]]
auc = {v: ev.value(v, "roc_auc")["value"] for v in releases}
seg = ev.segments()
ages = seg[(seg["factor"] == "age_band") & (seg["version"] == best)].set_index("segment")["share_called"]
cal = ev.calibration()
cal = cal[cal["version"] == best]
gap = (cal["mean_predicted"] - cal["observed_rate"]).abs().max()
expected = {
    3: f"{best} ranks the whole list best: ROC AUC {auc[best]:.3f}, against "
       f"{auc[releases[0]]:.3f} for {releases[0]}",
    4: f"{best} calls {ev.percent(ages.max())} of contacts aged {ages.idxmax()} but "
       f"{ev.percent(ages.min())} of those aged {ages.idxmin()}",
    5: f"{best}'s predicted probabilities are within {100 * gap:.1f} points of the observed rates",
}
text_holds(all(TITLES[i].replace("\u2019", "'") == t for i, t in expected.items())
           and TITLES[2].endswith(f"with the same {S['calls_made']:,} calls"),
           "the captured titles' numbers match outputs/")
meta = dict(re.findall(r'^(title|subtitle): "(.*)"$', deck, re.M))
alt_text_holds([TITLES[0], captured["subtitle"]] == [meta["title"], meta["subtitle"]] == [
    "Which release should the call centre use?",
    "The contact-ranking model, evaluated · Acme Signals (a fictional company)"], "fig-slides-title")

# The planted title: the runner-up's recall (the deck's rival) under the best release's name.
rival = ev.rival()
rival_recall = ev.value(rival, "recall_top10")["value"]
planted = headline.replace(ev.percent(recall), ev.percent(rival_recall))
text_holds(planted != headline and TITLES[2].startswith(f"{best} beats {rival} "),
           "the planted title and the comparison title beside it")
# Every prompt was dry-run, verbatim, by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) in a copy of checkpoint 15 on
# 2026-11-18. The PDF prompt was rewritten on 2026-11-24, when Chrome 158.0.8127.37 printed
# the deck from the command line as one blank page in 12 of 12 tries (6 with
# --run-all-compositor-stages-before-draw, 6 without); the script it asks for, which waits
# with Playwright for Reveal's print pages, printed all 8 pages in 12 of 12 (checkpoint 16 and
# examples/eval, which carry that script). Its dry runs are recorded beside the prompt.
```

The report and the model card are for people who read. The decision about which release
Acme's call centre will use is made somewhere else: in a meeting, in front of a screen, by
people who will look at each slide for a few seconds and remember perhaps three of them. One
of those three had better be the slide that says what is being decided, and on what
condition. A deck for that room is a different document: not a report cut into pieces, but a
short argument, one claim at a time, ending in the decision.

This chapter builds that deck for Acme's product team and its investors: a web page that
presents itself, a PDF to send afterwards and a PowerPoint file in the company's template, all
from one source that reads the same results as the report.

::: opener
- Name what makes a technical deck work, and the Reveal.js features that serve it: speaker
  notes, fragments, columns, themes and print view.
- Ask for a deck whose titles state claims computed from the results, guarded, with the detail
  in the notes.
- Check a theme's colours against WCAG's contrast minimum for normal text, with a test.
- Export the deck to PDF and to PowerPoint in a house template, and know what each format
  loses.

Start from
: your `acme-eval` repository at the end of @sec-results, or `checkpoints/15-eval-results/`.

You build
: `slides.qmd` as a Reveal.js deck, a PDF and a PowerPoint file, with a theme, a contrast test
  and a reference template.

Checkpoint
: `checkpoints/16-eval-slides/`
:::

Rendered from `checkpoints/16-eval-slides/slides.qmd`.](../media/figures/eval-deck-title.png){#fig-slides-title width=85% fig-alt="The title of a slide, Which release should the call centre use?, in bold navy on a warm off-white background, above its subtitle in dark ink: The contact-ranking model, evaluated, Acme Signals (a fictional company)."}

Read only its titles, and you have its argument:

```{python}
#| label: slides-titles
#| output: asis
print("\n".join(f"{i}. {title}" for i, title in enumerate(TITLES, start=1)))
```

## What makes a technical deck work {#sec-slides-good}

A deck succeeds when the room leaves knowing the claim, the evidence for it, and what was
decided. Five habits get it there, and each is something you can ask an agent for and check:

| Habit | You check |
|---|---|
| One claim per slide | no slide needs two sentences to say what it shows |
| The title states the claim, not "Results" | the titles alone, in order, are the argument |
| Numbers computed, words guarded | titles agree with `outputs/`; a guard stops a false one |
| Detail in the speaker notes | every slide has notes; no slide is a paragraph |
| End on the decision | the room knows what you are asking for |

: Five habits of a technical deck, and how to check each. {#tbl-slides-habits}

The second habit does the most work: it is why the titles at the start of this chapter make
the argument on their own, from the headline to the decision.

## What a deck can do, and what it is called {#sec-slides-vocab}

Quarto makes decks in two formats from one source: Reveal.js, a web page that presents
itself in any browser, and PowerPoint. Each `##` heading starts a slide in both. The rest is
vocabulary: features you ask for by name, on the screen and off it.

| Ask for | Quarto calls it |
|---|---|
| speaker notes | a `::: {.notes}` block on the slide |
| points revealed one at a time | *fragments*: `. . .` between paragraphs, or `::: {.fragment}` |
| two columns | `:::: {.columns}` holding `::: {.column width="50%"}` blocks |
| a slide with more text, smaller | the `{.smaller}` class on the heading |
| speaker view | press S while presenting |

: What a deck can show on the screen, and what Quarto calls it (Quarto 1.10.20). {#tbl-slides-vocab}

| Ask for | Quarto calls it |
|---|---|
| a theme | `theme: [default, acme.scss]`: a built-in theme and your Sass file |
| a footer and slide numbers | `footer:` and `slide-number: true` |
| a stable link to a slide | an ID on the heading: `## … {#decision}` |
| a PDF | the *print view*: press E, then print |
| a house PowerPoint template | `reference-doc:` naming a `.pptx` |

: How a deck looks and leaves the room. {#tbl-slides-export}

## The deck {#sec-slides-deck}

The prompt is the five habits and the vocabulary together, plus three phrases that steer round
traps met while testing it (@tbl-slides-phrases). It asks for one deck, as one task, because
its checks run without you: guards, the render, and the titles it lists.

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Create slides.qmd, a Reveal.js deck at 1280×720 for the product team and investors, from outputs/ only: a plain YAML title and subtitle (no inline code), then seven slides, one claim per slide, each slide's title stating its claim with any number as inline code, speaker notes on each of the seven, the ROC curves and who is called by age band as matplotlib figures with alt text and no `fig-` labels, a two-column slide comparing v2 and v3, and the caveats revealed one at a time. Guard every title whose wording depends on the results. Render it and list the slide titles.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `slides.qmd` · `uv run quarto render slides.qmd` → `slides.html`
:::

::: {.you}
open `slides.html` · press S for speaker view, and E for print view
:::

::: think
The agent says the deck rendered, and lists its titles. Two of them read
"`{python} planted`" and "`{python} TITLES[2]`". Which habits can a list of titles alone
prove, and is either title wrong?

From the list: that each title states a claim, and that the deck ends on a decision. Notes
need the slides; computed numbers and guards need the source. The first title is wrong:
`{python} ev.percent(rival_recall)` is `{python} rival`'s recall, the share of subscribers its
top tenth reaches, not `{python} best`'s. No
guard would stop it if the number were typed, which is why a title's numbers are inline code.
A title can also be computed and still read badly: one run printed `np.int64(6)`, a count taken straight from pandas. Read every
rendered title.

<!-- source: book/chapters/slides.qmd lines 152-153 at 651db10 ("a count printed straight from
pandas read `np.int64(6)` until it was converted to a plain `int`") -->
:::

**Read the titles first**, in the order the agent lists them: they should be the argument.
Then the source: each title's numbers are inline code, each claim in a title has a *guard*, a
check in the cell before it that stops the render once the claim is false, and each slide has a notes block. **Present it**: press S, and speaker
view opens in a second window with the notes, which is what you will see while the room sees
the slide.

::: story
<!-- source: book/chapters/slides.qmd lines 145–147 at 651db10 ("Notes written before the
first ## heading became an extra, blank slide"); the dry run is noted in this file's setup
cell. -->
While this deck was being built, the title slide's notes were written before the first `##`
heading. They became a slide of their own: an extra, blank one.
That is why the prompt asks for notes "on each of the seven", and why the finished deck
attaches the title's notes with a short filter, `filters/title-notes.lua`. Count the slides in
what comes back: there should be `{python} WORD[n_slides]`.
:::

| The prompt says | Because |
|---|---|
| "a plain YAML title" | inline code in `title` runs before any cell (`NameError`); with no title, the first heading is promoted, uncomputed |
| "no `fig-` labels" | a `fig-` label adds "Figure 1:" to the caption |
| "notes on each of the seven" | notes before the first `##` become a slide (the story above) |

: Why the deck prompt says what it says. {#tbl-slides-phrases}

::: pitfall
Look at every slide at the deck's size. In one test run a `fig-dpi` setting gave the figures a
fixed size that overflowed the slide; in another, with no such setting, they filled less than
half of it. The finished deck's theme gives figures a fixed height.

<!-- source: book/chapters/slides.qmd lines 149-151 at 651db10 ("a `fig-dpi` setting gave
figures a fixed size that overflowed the slide; in another run, with no such setting, the
figures filled less than half of it") -->
:::

## A theme you can read {#sec-slides-theme}

A theme is where a deck's colours and fonts live, and it is where most decks fail their
audience: pale grey text on white is unreadable on a projector. The Web Content
Accessibility Guidelines set the minimum: a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 between normal text and
its background, 3 to 1 for large text (WCAG 2.2, success criterion 1.4.3). The book's test holds
every colour to the stricter figure, since a slide's smaller text is normal text. A test can check it, so ask for the test with
the theme:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add acme.scss, a Reveal.js theme on top of `default`: dark ink on a warm off-white background, a navy for headings and links, system fonts. Add tests/test_deck_contrast.py checking that body text and links have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 on the background (WCAG 2.2), run it, and render the deck.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `acme.scss` and the test · `uv run pytest` · renders the deck
:::

The finished theme's colours, measured with the guideline's formula:

```{python}
#| output: asis
lines = ["| Text | Colour | Contrast on the background |", "|---|---|--:|"]
lines += [f"| {role} | `{colour[role]}` | {ratios[role]:.1f}:1 |" for role in ROLES]
print("\n".join(lines))
print(f"\n: The finished theme's text colours on its background, `{paper}`, computed with the WCAG 2.2 formula, from the variables its test checks. {{#tbl-slides-contrast}}")
```

The test makes the rule permanent: a later change of colour that fails it fails the test
suite, before anyone squints at a projector. One thing a theme does not reach: matplotlib draws
its figures on white, which shows as a white box on an off-white slide. The finished deck
draws them on a transparent background. Colour is not the only part of a readable deck,
so keep the other habits too: figure labels legible from the back of the room, colours that
differ in lightness as well as hue, and alt text on every figure.

## A PDF to send afterwards {#sec-slides-pdf}

After the meeting, someone will ask for the slides. Quarto 1.10.20 has no PDF format for
Reveal.js decks; the route is Reveal.js's print view, printed by a browser. By hand, open the
deck, press E, and print to PDF. To make it part of the build, a script can do the same in
the Chrome you already have, and check its own result:

<!-- Dry-run 2026-11-24, verbatim, in a copy of checkpoint 16 without scripts/deck_pdf.py or
Playwright, the deck rendered: a Claude Code sub-agent on Sonnet 5.5 and one on Haiku 5.5 each
added Playwright as a dev dependency with uv, wrote the script and printed 8 pages, one per slide, on the first
try (Chrome 158.0.8127.37). The lead checked each PDF: 8 pages of 1056 × 594 pt (Reveal's print
page for a 1280 × 720 deck, with its margin), none blank. -->
::: {.prompt}
```default
Write scripts/deck_pdf.py: open slides.html at `?print-pdf` in the installed Chrome with Playwright (a dev dependency), wait until the page holds one `.pdf-page` per slide, print it to slides.pdf, check that the PDF has one page per slide, and retry up to three times if it does not. Run it and tell me the page count.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`uv add --dev playwright` · writes `scripts/deck_pdf.py` · `uv run python scripts/deck_pdf.py` → `slides.pdf`
:::

::: story
<!-- source: book/chapters/slides.qmd lines 204–210 at 651db10; REVISION-PLAN.md lines
546–548; and the test of 2026-11-24 recorded in this file's setup cell. The records give
different rates, so the story quotes none (PLAN-improvement-briefs.md §5). -->
The first version of this script printed from Chrome's command line, the obvious way. It
wrote the deck as a PDF of a single blank page: Chrome had printed before the deck laid itself
out. The script's check, one page per slide, caught every blank print.
:::

So the script waits for what it needs. Reveal.js builds its print view a moment after the
page loads, one page per slide; Playwright, a library that drives a browser from Python, opens
the deck in your Chrome, waits until those pages exist, and only then prints. Tested for this
book on 2026-11-24 with Chrome 158.0.8127.37, the command line printed a blank page every
time, with or without Chrome's flag for finishing the drawing first; the script printed every
slide every time. Keep the check anyway, because the next browser may change again: a page
count that must equal the slide count catches a blank print, and a slide too tall for its
page, which Reveal.js prints on two.

## PowerPoint, in the house template {#sec-slides-pptx}

Many organisations circulate decks as PowerPoint, in a template with their colours, fonts
and logo. Quarto renders PowerPoint from the same source, and a *reference document* carries
the template: a `.pptx` file whose theme and slide layouts Quarto copies. Start from Quarto's
own, so that its layouts have the names Quarto expects:

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Add a PowerPoint version: make templates/acme-reference.pptx from Quarto's default (`quarto pandoc -o templates/acme-reference.pptx --print-default-data-file reference.pptx`) with a script that sets its theme colours and font to the deck's, add pptx to slides.qmd with `reference-doc`, render, and check the slide count and the theme colours in the file.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`quarto pandoc -o templates/acme-reference.pptx …` · writes a script that edits the template's theme · renders `slides.pptx` · counts slides, reads the theme
:::

Your organisation's own template works as a reference document if its layouts carry the names
Quarto uses: Title Slide, Title and Content, Section Header, Two Content, Comparison, Content
with Caption and Blank; rename them in the slide master if not. A template is a binary file,
so commit the script that makes it too:
the script can be reviewed in a diff, and the file cannot.

Know what PowerPoint keeps and what it loses. Speaker notes go to its notes pane, and two
columns to its Two Content layout. The theme's Sass rules do not apply, fragments become
static lists, `.smaller` and the footer do nothing, and Quarto 1.10.20 writes the image's file
name where the figure's alt text should be; the finished project adds it back with a short
script after the render. Open the PowerPoint file and check each slide, as its reader will.

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/16-eval-slides/README.md
```
:::

::: tryit
Build the deck, its theme and test, the PDF and the PowerPoint file, and present the deck once
in speaker view.

::: done
the titles read as the argument; every slide after the title has notes; the contrast test passes; the PDF has
one page per slide; and the PowerPoint file opens in the template's colours.
:::
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- A technical deck is a short argument: one claim per slide, each title stating it, the detail
  in the notes, and the decision on the last slide.
- Ask for features by name: speaker notes, fragments, columns, a theme, print view, a
  reference document.
- A title's numbers are computed and its words are guarded, like any sentence in a report.
- Check colours with a contrast test, against WCAG's 4.5:1 minimum for normal text, so a readable deck
  stays readable.
- PDF comes from print view, checked page by page; PowerPoint comes from a reference document,
  and loses the theme, fragments and alt text, so open it before you send it.
:::

The deck makes the case once, in a room. The results also need a place where anyone can find
them, in the company's colours, with every document linked: a site.
